Page 3

Warm Up

The warm-up asks students to identify the similar matrix decomposition (SMD) corresponding to the following geometric transformation:

  • Stretch by a factor of 3 in the \(\vec{v}_1\)-direction, and
  • Stretch by a factor of 2 in the \(\vec{v}_2\)-direction.

This gives the SMD:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2\\2 & 4\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}3 & 0\\0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2\\2 & 4\end{bmatrix}^{-1} \]
The GeoGebra applet shows a coordinate grid overlaid with a basis grid formed by \(\vec{v}_1\) and \(\vec{v}_2\). The original unit square \(S_B\) (in red) and its image \(T(S_B)\) (in blue) are shown. The transformation stretches the unit square by factors of 3 and 2 along the two basis directions, producing a larger diamond-shaped region. Labeled points include \(Q'\) at approximately \((0, 15)\), \(P'\) at approximately \((6, 7)\), \(R'\) at approximately \((-9, 8)\), and \(T(S_B)\) labeled near the center.

Page 4

Warm Up (continued)

The second part of the warm-up involves a shear transformation:

  • Shear the vector \(\vec{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}-3\\1\end{bmatrix}\) by \(-1\) unit in the \(\vec{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}2\\3\end{bmatrix}\) direction.

This gives the SMD:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & -3\\3 & 1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\\0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}2 & -3\\3 & 1\end{bmatrix}^{-1} \]
The GeoGebra applet shows the basis vectors \(\vec{v}_1\) (in red) and \(\vec{v}_2\) (in blue) with the original unit square \(S_B\) (red shading) and its sheared image \(T(S_B)\) (blue shading). The shear moves the \(\vec{v}_2\) direction by \(-1\) unit along \(\vec{v}_1\), leaving \(\vec{v}_1\) fixed. Labeled points include \(Q'\) at approximately \((-3, 4)\), \(P'\) at approximately \((3, 3)\), and \(R'\) at approximately \((-3, -2)\).

Page 5

“Simple” Systems – Linear Algebra Version

Let the standard basis vectors be \(\vec{e}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\vec{e}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\).

NameSystem (Matrix Form)General Solution
Uncoupled \(\vec{r}\,' = \begin{bmatrix}a & 0\\0 & b\end{bmatrix}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = C\,\vec{e}_1\,e^{at} + D\,\vec{e}_2\,e^{bt}\)
Partially Coupled \(\vec{r}\,' = \begin{bmatrix}a & 1\\0 & a\end{bmatrix}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = \bigl(C\,\vec{e}_1 + D(\vec{e}_1\,t + \vec{e}_2)\bigr)e^{at}\)
Complex Uncoupled \(\vec{r}\,' = \begin{bmatrix}a & -b\\b & a\end{bmatrix}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = C_1\bigl(\cos(bt)\,\vec{e}_1 + \sin(bt)\,\vec{e}_2\bigr)e^{at} + C_2\bigl(-\sin(bt)\,\vec{e}_1 + \cos(bt)\,\vec{e}_2\bigr)e^{at}\)

Goal: any system \(\vec{r}\,' = A\vec{r}\) reduces to one of these three types via an SMD.

Page 6

SMDs and First-Order Systems

Fact: Every 2×2 matrix \(A\) can be written as \(A = PBP^{-1}\) for some matrix \(P\) and some \(B\) of one of the three simple types:

\[ B = \begin{bmatrix}a & 0\\0 & b\end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix}a & 1\\0 & a\end{bmatrix}, \quad \text{or} \quad B = \begin{bmatrix}a & -b\\b & a\end{bmatrix}. \]

We will use this fact to solve general first-order linear systems.

Page 7

SMDs and First-Order Systems – Derivation

Let \(A = PBP^{-1}\), where \(P = [\vec{v}_1 \mid \vec{v}_2]\) and \(B\) is one of the three simple types.

Starting from \(\vec{r}\,' = A\vec{r}\), substitute \(A = PBP^{-1}\):

\[ \vec{r}\,' = PBP^{-1}\vec{r} \]

Multiply both sides on the left by \(P^{-1}\):

\[ P^{-1}\vec{r}\,' = BP^{-1}\vec{r} \]

Let \(\vec{s} = P^{-1}\vec{r}\). Then \(\vec{s}\,' = P^{-1}\vec{r}\,'\), so:

\[ \vec{s}\,' = B\vec{s} \]

The substitution \(\vec{s} = P^{-1}\vec{r}\) reduces the system to the simple form \(\vec{s}\,' = B\vec{s}\).

Page 8

SMDs and First-Order Systems – Substitution Variables

Write \(P^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}\alpha & \beta \\ \gamma & \delta\end{bmatrix}\). Then \(\vec{s} = P^{-1}\vec{r}\) gives:

\[ \vec{s} = \begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix} = P^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\alpha x + \beta y \\ \gamma x + \delta y\end{bmatrix} \]

So the substitution is:

\[ u = \alpha x + \beta y, \qquad v = \gamma x + \delta y. \]

Page 9

SMDs and First-Order Systems – Recovery

With \(\vec{s} = \begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix}\), the reduced system is \(\vec{s}\,' = B\vec{s}\).

Once \(\vec{s}(t)\) is found, recover \(\vec{r}(t)\) by:

\[ P^{-1}\vec{r} = \vec{s} \implies \vec{r} = P\vec{s}. \]

Page 10

SMDs and First-Order Systems – Recovery via \(P\)

Since \(P^{-1}\vec{r} = \vec{s}\), we have \(\vec{r} = P\vec{s}\).

To see what this produces in terms of \(\vec{v}_1\) and \(\vec{v}_2\), recall:

\[ P\vec{e}_1 = \vec{v}_1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad P\vec{e}_2 = \vec{v}_2. \]

Note: Matrix multiplication distributes over sums, and scalars factor out. These two facts allow us to replace every \(\vec{e}_i\) in the solution with \(\vec{v}_i\) after applying \(P\).

Page 11

SMDs and First-Order Systems – Uncoupled Case

For the uncoupled case, the simple system \(\vec{s}\,' = \begin{bmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{bmatrix}\vec{s}\) has solution:

\[ \vec{s}(t) = C\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}e^{at} + D\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}e^{bt} = C\,\vec{e}_1\,e^{at} + D\,\vec{e}_2\,e^{bt}. \]

Recovering \(\vec{r} = P\vec{s}\):

\[ \vec{r}(t) = P\bigl(C\,\vec{e}_1\,e^{at} + D\,\vec{e}_2\,e^{bt}\bigr) = C\,P\vec{e}_1\,e^{at} + D\,P\vec{e}_2\,e^{bt} = C\,\vec{v}_1\,e^{at} + D\,\vec{v}_2\,e^{bt}. \]

Every \(\vec{e}_i\) in the standard-basis solution is replaced by the corresponding \(\vec{v}_i\).

Page 12

Systems – Linear Algebra Version (General Basis)

Let \(\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2\) be basis vectors with change-of-basis matrix \(P = [\vec{v}_1 \mid \vec{v}_2]\).

NameSystemGeneral Solution
Uncoupled \(\vec{r}\,' = P\begin{bmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{bmatrix}P^{-1}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = C\,\vec{v}_1\,e^{at} + D\,\vec{v}_2\,e^{bt}\)
Partially Coupled \(\vec{r}\,' = P\begin{bmatrix}a&1\\0&a\end{bmatrix}P^{-1}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = \bigl(C\,\vec{v}_1 + D(\vec{v}_1\,t + \vec{v}_2)\bigr)e^{at}\)
Complex Uncoupled \(\vec{r}\,' = P\begin{bmatrix}a&-b\\b&a\end{bmatrix}P^{-1}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = C_1\bigl(\cos(bt)\,\vec{v}_1 + \sin(bt)\,\vec{v}_2\bigr)e^{at} + C_2\bigl(-\sin(bt)\,\vec{v}_1 + \cos(bt)\,\vec{v}_2\bigr)e^{at}\)

Note: All \(\vec{e}_i\)’s become \(\vec{v}_i\)’s.

Page 13

Examples – Uncoupled Saddle

The system is:

\[ \vec{x}\,' = PDP^{-1}\vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}-3&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}^{-1}\vec{x} = \begin{bmatrix}-4x+3y\\-2x+3y\end{bmatrix} \]

Parameters: \(a = -3\), \(b = 2\).

This is an uncoupled saddle: flow moves in along the \(\vec{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix}\) direction (eigenvalue \(-3 < 0\)) and out along the \(\vec{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}\) direction (eigenvalue \(2 > 0\)).

The GeoGebra phase portrait shows a vector field with two invariant lines (dashed blue) along \(\vec{v}_1\) and \(\vec{v}_2\). Solution trajectories flow inward along the \(\vec{v}_1\)-line toward the origin and outward along the \(\vec{v}_2\)-line away from it. The coordinate grid (dotted lines) is aligned with the basis \(\{\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2\}\). A particular solution curve (purple) is shown bending from the \(\vec{v}_1\)-direction toward the \(\vec{v}_2\)-direction. The basis vectors \(\vec{v}_1\) (red arrow at \((1,1)\)) and \(\vec{v}_2\) (purple arrow) are drawn at the origin.

Page 14

Examples – Partially Coupled Sink

The system is:

\[ \vec{x}\,' = PDP^{-1}\vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}-0.2&1\\0&-0.2\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}^{-1}\vec{x} = \begin{bmatrix}-0.8x+1.8y\\-0.2x+0.4y\end{bmatrix} \]

Parameter: \(a = -0.2\).

This is a partially coupled sink: all trajectories flow in along the \(\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix}\)-direction, tangent to the invariant line.

The GeoGebra phase portrait shows a repeated-eigenvalue sink. The single invariant line (dashed blue) runs along \(\vec{v}_1\). Solution trajectories spiral inward toward the origin, becoming parallel to \(\vec{v}_1\) as \(t \to \infty\). A particular solution starting near \((0, 2)\) curves inward along the invariant line direction. Basis vectors \(\vec{v}_1\) (red) and \(\vec{v}_2\) (blue) are shown at the origin.

Page 15

Examples – Spiral Sink

The system is:

\[ \vec{x}\,' = PDP^{-1}\vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}-0.2&-2\\2&-0.2\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}^{-1}\vec{x} = \begin{bmatrix}1.8x - 4y\\2x - 2.2y\end{bmatrix} \]

Parameters: \(a = -0.2\), \(b = 2\).

This is a spiral sink: trajectories spiral inward relative to the basis \(\left\{\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}\right\}\).

The GeoGebra phase portrait shows inward-spiraling solution curves (purple) converging toward the origin. The spiraling occurs relative to the coordinate grid defined by the basis \(\{\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2\}\) (dotted lines), not the standard axes. The basis vectors \(\vec{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix}\) (red arrow near \((2,1)\)) and \(\vec{v}_2\) (purple arrow) are drawn at the origin. The dashed blue line shows the axis of the \(B\)-coordinate grid.

Page 16

Eigentheory

If we know \(A = PBP^{-1}\), we know the general solution. So it remains to answer: given \(A\), how do we find \(P\) and \(B\)?

Idea: Look for invariant lines – lines through the origin that are mapped to themselves by the transformation \(T_A\).

There are different types of invariant lines depending on the type of \(B\) (uncoupled, partially coupled, or complex uncoupled).

Page 17

Eigentheory – Algebraic Condition

We look for nonzero vectors \(\vec{v}\) such that:

\[ A\vec{v} = \lambda\vec{v} \]

for some scalar \(\lambda\). Rearranging:

\[ A\vec{v} - \lambda\vec{v} = \vec{0} \implies (A - \lambda I)\vec{v} = \vec{0}. \]

For a nonzero solution \(\vec{v}\) to exist, the matrix \((A - \lambda I)\) cannot be invertible.

Characteristic Equation: The condition for a nonzero solution is:

\[ \det(A - \lambda I) = 0. \]

The values \(\lambda\) satisfying this equation are called eigenvalues of \(A\), and the corresponding nonzero vectors \(\vec{v}\) are called eigenvectors.
